text: Is There a Way to Measure Cortisol Levels? Blood, Urine, Saliva and Home Kits. Yes. Cortisol, the body's main stress hormone, can be measured with a cortisol test that checks blood, urine or saliva. Doctors order these tests through a lab, and consumers can also buy at-home kits that they mail back for analysis.. Consumer at-home cortisol tests and wearable stress trackers are drawing attention as more Americans seek ways to check their stress hormone without a doctor's visit. WebMD updated its guide in February 2026, and Cleveland Clinic's guide was last updated in April 2025.. Doctors usually order the test when symptoms suggest that cortisol is either too high or too low. Blood draws are the most common method, and a typical adult blood test at a lab chain costs around $72, according to WebMD. The at-home version runs about $130, and at-home cortisol tests in general range from about $50 to $400. Home kits use a finger-prick blood sample, a saliva sample or a urine sample. Buyers collect the sample, mail it to the lab that sold the kit, and read results in an online account, usually within one to seven days depending on the product. Healthline lists one saliva kit at $86 with results in five to seven days, and another at $149 with results in two to five days. Some labs let people visit a location where a technician draws the sample, which WebMD says is often cheaper than a home kit. Because cortisol rises and falls across the day, a single reading can miss the pattern. Cleveland Clinic notes that results can take one to five days, and that a person may need to be tested twice in one day or several times over a number of days. Clinicians also warn that a home test is not a diagnosis; WebMD recommends seeing a doctor for the most accurate result. A newer category, continuous wearable sensors, is still in development. One company, Auromone, says its Curve device is designed to read cortisol from sweat, but it is not yet a diagnostic tool and has not been cleared for medical use.
